title: Inventory Privacy: What to Tell Family and What Never to Write Down
plain:
No — do not tell anyone what you found or how much there is — not yet. This is not about distrusting your sister. Until the wallet is verified and secured, an unconfirmed number can cause arguments, pressure, and safety risks, and early guesses about value are often wrong anyway.

If she asks, tell family only that records exist and you are working through them carefully. That answer is honest and true. Wait until the wallet is verified and an attorney advises you before any numbers or details go to anyone, including close relatives.

The same privacy rule applies to your Day 2 inventory sheet. Never copy the words into your inventory — not the full 24, not part of them, not a hint of them. Those words are the money itself: anyone who reads them can move everything, and an inventory page is exactly the kind of document that gets carried around, shown to helpers, or left on a table.

Instead, write only a description like '24-word list found, sealed envelope, 3 pages'. Record where each item was found, what it looks like, and its condition — never its contents. The inventory page must contain no secrets: no recovery words, no passwords, no PINs, no amounts.
technical:
Disclosure control: treat both the balance and the existence of recovery material as confidential during the inheritance inventory. Sharing of amounts is deferred until two conditions are met — the wallet has been verified against its backup, and an attorney has advised on the estate process. Until then, family communications state only that records exist and are being reviewed carefully.

Inventory hygiene: the inventory document records metadata only — location, medium (paper, card, hardware wallet), word count (12 or 24), and physical condition. Recovery words, passphrases, and PINs are never transcribed, dictated, or photographed into the inventory or stored digitally anywhere; the inventory page must contain no secrets. Recovery words function as a bearer instrument: anyone who obtains them controls the funds.
